analysis.one_liner: Repeals Medicaid work requirements, immigrant eligibility limits, and provider tax restrictions enacted in 2025.
analysis.headline: A single House Democrat introduced a bill to repeal the 2025 law's Medicaid cuts, including work requirements; it had zero cosponsors and was referred to two committees with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would undo the Medicaid portions of the 2025 tax-and-spending law. That would end the new work and community-service requirements for the Medicaid expansion population, restore federal payment for care for lawfully present immigrants and certain other residents, and lift the new limits on how states finance their Medicaid share through provider taxes. In short, it would put Medicaid rules back to what they were before the 2025 law passed.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income adults on Medicaid expansion coverage who would otherwise have to document work or community service to keep it; lawfully present immigrants and other residents who would regain federal coverage for services; hospitals, especially rural ones, that would see less uncompensated care; and states that use provider taxes to finance their Medicaid share. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the requirement that people in the Medicaid expansion population perform work, community service, or similar activities to qualify for coverage, so enrollees would not lose insurance over paperwork or hours requirements.
It restores federal Medicaid and CHIP payment for services to lawfully present immigrants and other covered residents, reversing restrictions that begin in fiscal year 2027.
It lifts the new limits on Medicaid provider taxes that start in fiscal year 2027, giving states back a financing tool many use to fund their share of the program.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, because repealing these provisions undoes major federal spending cuts in the 2025 law and increases projected deficits; supporters of the original restrictions also argue that repealing work and eligibility rules weakens program integrity checks. [S2]
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, through higher Medicaid spending

drawbacks.text: Repealing the restrictions on federal payment for non-citizens and lifting provider tax limits would increase federal Medicaid spending and deficits; the 2025 provisions were written to reduce federal costs.

The bill restores pre-2025 policy wholesale rather than rewriting it: it keeps no version of the work requirements or eligibility verification that supporters of the 2025 law said protected the program from waste, so the debate over those rules simply returns to zero.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of people on Medicaid, the benefit is direct: no work paperwork to keep coverage and restored eligibility for lawfully present immigrants, and hospitals gain when fewer patients show up uninsured. The cost is real and concentrated at the federal level: the provisions being repealed were among the largest sources of savings in the 2025 law, so repealing them raises deficits and restarts the argument over whether work rules and provider tax limits curb waste or simply cut people off. The bill does not attempt a compromise between those positions; it simply restores the old rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to two House committees, which have taken no action on it; Congress is still in session, so its fate is not yet final.

narrative.text: Representative Brendan Boyle introduced the bill in the House on July 9, 2026, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee; neither committee has held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor.
The bill would repeal chapter 1 of subtitle B of title VII of the 2025 reconciliation law, restoring the laws that chapter amended as if that chapter had never been enacted.
The current Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill technically remains alive, but with zero cosponsors and no committee action months before the session ends, it has not moved at all.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has acted on the bill, which means the Medicaid cuts in the 2025 law remain on the books; opponents of repeal are ahead by default, while Medicaid enrollees facing the work requirements and eligibility restrictions get no relief.

for.name: Rep. Brendan Boyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Medicaid provisions of the 2025 reconciliation law and referred it to two committees.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or floor consideration has occurred.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority controlling the House floor schedule
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a vote; no Republican cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: There have been no votes, but the bill's only support is its Democratic sponsor, with zero cosponsors of either party, in a chamber controlled by Republicans who passed the 2025 law it would amend.

industries.note: Repealing the eligibility restrictions and work requirements means more enrolled, insured patients and less unpaid care, and repealing the provider tax limits restores supplemental payments many hospitals rely on. Rural hospitals are typically the most exposed when Medicaid coverage is cut.

States regain the provider tax tool to finance their Medicaid share, but they also bear more program costs as federal eligibility restrictions come off. Many states pushed back against the 2025 restrictions.
Insurers that administer Medicaid coverage would keep more enrollees if the work requirements and eligibility restrictions were repealed, since enrollment would not drop under the new rules.

analysis.trajectory: This bill is unlikely to advance. A one-sponsor repeal bill with no cosponsors, introduced in July of an election-year session and referred to two committees with no subsequent action, almost always dies in committee when the Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Undoing parts of the 2025 law would also require action in the Republican-controlled House and Senate, which is not happening.
